::: {.chapter-lead}
This page does not reintroduce tokenization, the next-token distribution, or likelihood as foundational concepts: those have canonical lessons. It deepens two mathematical connections: the chain rule that justifies autoregressive factorization, and the relationship between soft-target cross-entropy and KL divergence.
:::

::: {.callout-note .learning-outcomes collapse="true" title="Learning outcomes"}
By the end of this page, you will be able to:
- derive autoregressive factorization from the probability chain rule;
- distinguish a probabilistic identity from the parameterized model that approximates its conditionals;
- briefly connect likelihood, log-likelihood, and the training objective;
- derive the identity between cross-entropy, target entropy, and KL divergence;
- state the assumptions, direction, and cases in which these quantities become infinite.
:::

## 1. From the chain rule to autoregressive factorization

The [output probabilities](probabilities.qmd) lesson defines the conditional probability of the next token, \(P(x_t\mid x_{<t})\), and explains how the model constructs its distribution. Here, we use that quantity to derive the probability of a complete sequence.

For any joint distribution, the probability chain rule gives:

\[
P(x_1,\ldots,x_T)
=P(x_1)P(x_2\mid x_1)\cdots
P(x_T\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{T-1}).
\]

Writing \(x_{<t}=(x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1})\), we obtain:

\[
\boxed{
P(x_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P(x_t\mid x_{<t})
}
\]

This is the **autoregressive factorization**: the sequence probability is the product of the conditional probabilities of its tokens, in order.

**The chain rule is a probabilistic identity**, valid for any joint distribution. It does not by itself impose an architecture or a particular computation order. The autoregressive aspect comes from the model that represents and uses the conditionals in prefix order: at position \(t\), the token is predicted from preceding tokens, not future tokens.

For the first token, the prefix is empty. In practice, a beginning-of-sequence token (BOS) may be explicit, or an equivalent convention may be used.

## 2. From a parameterized model to the training objective

A model with parameters (	heta) approximates the conditionals:

\[
P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]

The factorization then implies:

\[
P_\theta(x_{1:T})
=\prod_{t=1}^{T}P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}),
\qquad
\log P_\theta(x_{1:T})
=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log P_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}).
\]

Maximum likelihood seeks to increase the log-likelihood of observed sequences; its minimized form is negative log-likelihood (NLL). This equivalence does not determine reduction over tokens and examples, or how padding and ignored positions are handled. Those conventions belong to the canonical lessons on [likelihood](likelihood.qmd), [cross-entropy](cross-entropy.qmd), and aggregated [loss](loss.qmd).

**Notation bridge.** Probabilistic lessons often use \(P\) for an event probability or conditional distribution. Computational lessons use (p_{b,t,v}) for component (v) of the probability vector at example (b) and position (t). The target ID (y_{b,t}) selects (p_{b,t,y_{b,t}}). These are compatible levels of description, not different probabilistic objects.

## 3. Soft targets and KL divergence

One-hot targets place all mass on a single category. Some methods instead use a target distribution (q)—for example, label smoothing or a distribution supplied by a teacher model—over the (V) tokens.

For a target distribution (q) and predicted distribution (p), cross-entropy is:

\[
H(q,p)=-\sum_{i=1}^{V}q_i\log p_i.
\]

Terms with \(q_i=0\) contribute zero. With a one-hot target, the sum reduces to \(-\log p_y\); with a soft target, multiple categories contribute. Assume \(q_i\geq 0\), \(\sum_i q_i=1\), and that \(p\) is also normalized. Unless stated otherwise, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm, so losses are measured in nats; using \(\log_2\) gives bits.

Define target entropy as \(H(q)=-\sum_i q_i\log q_i\). The identity

\[
H(q,p)=H(q)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)
\]

explains why, for a fixed target (q), minimizing cross-entropy with respect to (p) is equivalent to minimizing KL divergence toward that target. For finite quantities, the identity follows directly from the definitions:

\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)
&=\sum_i q_i\log\frac{q_i}{p_i}\\
&=\sum_i q_i\log q_i-\sum_i q_i\log p_i\\
&=-H(q)+H(q,p).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(H(q,p)=H(q)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)\).

Here, \(q\) and \(p\) are normalized distributions and zero-mass terms contribute zero. If \(q_i>0\) but \(p_i=0\), cross-entropy and \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)\) are infinite under the usual extended-value convention. KL divergence is **directional**; cross-entropy is neither symmetric nor a metric distance.

For example, with (q=(1,0)) and (p=(0.9,0.1)):

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)=-\log(0.9)\approx 0.105\text{ nats},
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)=+\infty.
\]

The second quantity is infinite because (p) assigns positive mass to a category to which (q) assigns zero mass. In numerical computation, a stable log-softmax implementation helps avoid accidental underflow; it does not change this mathematical condition.

The [Cross-entropy](cross-entropy.qmd) lesson remains the canonical home for per-token loss, the one-hot case, masks, and reduction conventions. This advanced page focuses on the derivation and the general soft-target case.

## What this formalization does not determine

- **The tokenizer:** text segmentation and vocabulary are covered in [text and data](text-data.qmd) and [tokenization strategies](tokenization-strategies.qmd).
- **The architecture:** probabilistic factorization alone does not imply a Transformer.
- **Truth of outputs:** a high probability is not factual validation.
- **Generation strategy:** sampling and greedy selection occur after the distribution is computed ([generation](generation.qmd)).

- Bishop, *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning*, Chapters 1–2, for probabilistic foundations.
